arXiv:2509.10363v1 [cs.LG] 12 Sep 2025

PHYSICS-INFORMED SENSOR COVERAGE THROUGH STRUCTURE PRESERVING DATA-DRIVEN MODELS

Benjamin D. Shaffer    Brooks Kinch    Joseph Klobusicky    M. Ani Hsieh    and Nathaniel Trask
Abstract

We present a machine learning framework for adaptive source localization in which agents use a structure-preserving digital twin of a coupled hydrodynamic-transport system for real-time trajectory planning and data assimilation. The twin is constructed with conditional neural Whitney forms, coupling the numerical guarantees of finite element exterior calculus with transformer based operator learning. The resulting model preserves discrete conservation, and adapts in real time to streaming sensor data. It employs a conditional attention mechanism to identify: a reduced Whitney-form basis; reduced integral balance equations; and a source field, each compatible with given sensor measurements. The induced reduced-order environmental model retains the stability and consistency of standard finite-element simulation, yielding a physically realizable, regular mapping from sensor data to the source field. We propose a staggered scheme that alternates between evaluating the digital twin and applying Lloyd’s algorithm to guide sensor placement, with analysis providing conditions for monotone improvement of a coverage functional. Using the predicted source field as an importance function within an optimal-recovery scheme, we demonstrate recovery of point sources under continuity assumptions, highlighting the role of regularity as a sufficient condition for localization. Experimental comparisons with physics-agnostic transformer architectures show improved accuracy in complex geometries when physical constraints are enforced, indicating that structure preservation provides an effective inductive bias for source identification.

keywords
Optimal coverage, Digital twins, Operator learning, Adaptive sampling, Inverse problems, Structure preservation, Physics-informed machine learning, Data-driven modeling

1 Abstract Problem Definition

We consider a physical system governed by a steady-state coupled hydrodynamic–passive scalar transport process:

ℳ⁡(𝐯)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{v}) =0,\displaystyle=0, (1)
∇⋅ℱ⁡(u,𝐯)\displaystyle\nabla\cdot\mathcal{F}(u,\mathbf{v}) =fin Ω,\displaystyle=f\quad\text{in }\Omega, (2)

where ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes a hydrodynamic model that generates the velocity field 𝐯\mathbf{v} (e.g., satisfying Navier–Stokes or Darcy), and ℱ\mathcal{F} is the transport flux of a conserved density uu, whose divergence balances the source ff. The system is subject to appropriate boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega for both hydrodynamics and transport.

We consider a set of agents X={xi​(t)}i=1NX=\{x_{i}(t)\}_{i=1}^{N} that provide pointwise sensor measurements zi=u⁡(xi​(t))z_{i}=u(x_{i}(t)). We formulate a distributed control problem in which sensor dynamics are prescribed to optimally estimate an unknown source field ff. Central to this control problem is the properties of the inverse map 𝐳↦(u,f)\mathbf{z}\mapsto(u,f). Our hypothesis is that structure-preserving, data-driven models encoding reduced-order predictions of Eq. (1) yield improved performance compared to physics-agnostic surrogates which treat the mapping 𝐳↦(u,f)\mathbf{z}\mapsto(u,f) exclusively as a supervised regression problem.

We achieve this objective by constructing an adaptable, deployable digital twin, a data-driven reduced-order model supporting real-time inference and data assimilation. Specifically, we introduce by ansatz a conservation law of the form

ℋ⁡(u,θ,z):=∇⋅ℱθ​(u,z)−fθ​(z)=0,\mathcal{H}(u;\theta,z):=\nabla\cdot\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(u,z)-f_{\theta}(z)=0, (3)

where ℱθ​(u,z)\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(u,z) is a learnable flux and fθ​(z)f_{\theta}(z) is a learnable source term, both conditioned on sensor input zz; we generically denote learnable operators throughout using θ\theta. To construct a reduced-order finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) basis compatible with this ansatz, we employ our recently developed Conditional Neural Whitney Forms (CNWF) [36]. The reduced basis, flux, and source are trained offline in concert to obtain a parametric model that (1) can be solved in real time and (2) can specialize these three learnable components to different sensor readings.

Specifically, we assume the flux operator ℱ\mathcal{F} and the source field ff are unknown, and that we have access only to sparse and noisy measurements of the state uu, obtained through an observation function 𝒪\mathcal{O}, yielding sensor data z=𝒪⁡(u)z=\mathcal{O}(u). We distinguish offline training and online deployment. Offline, we assume access to data pairs of the state and observations, {(zi,ui,fi)}i=1D\{(z_{i},u_{i},f_{i})\}_{i=1}^{D}. During deployment, each observation zz conditions the learned physics, recalibrating the PDE operator in real time without retraining and thereby fulfilling the closed-loop requirements of a digital twin [69].

To identify the parameters θ\theta, we solve a PDE-constrained optimization problem:

minθ⁡ℒ⁡(u,θ,z)subject toℋ⁡(u,θ,z)=0,\min_{\theta}\;\mathcal{L}(u,\theta,z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathcal{H}(u;\theta,z)=0, (4)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is a loss functional that penalizes prediction error and enforces consistency with the sensor data. Data can be continuously generated by sampling random sensor configurations and providing compatible (u,f)(u,f) fields.

Our digital twin approach supports adaptive sensor placement by leveraging the predicted source field fθ​(z)f_{\theta}(z) to inform the repositioning of mobile sensors; we prescribe a policy for agents of the form

x˙i=G⁡(f),\dot{x}_{i}=G(f), (5)

where FF is a prescribed optimal coverage functional designed to move sensors toward the source while maintaining quasi-uniform coverage over the support of ff. This establishes a closed-loop interaction between observation, inference, and data acquisition. The model can then be refined through active feedback.

We consider two hypotheses:

H1 Physics-based constraints in the digital twin impose inductive biases that induce a more regular and accurate inverse mapping from sensor data to the source field. H2 In the optimal coverage problem, regularity in the sensor-to-source map improves source recovery.

2 Motivation

Many sensing tasks of scientific and engineering interest, such as locating pollution sources, tracking environmental hazards, or monitoring industrial processes, require measurements in dynamic and uncertain environments. In these settings, static sensor networks are often inefficient or infeasible, and the ability to reposition sensors in response to evolving knowledge of the environment is critical. Mobile sensor platforms, when paired with deployable digital twins, that is, computational models that can be updated in real time using incoming data, establish an iterative loop of prediction, measurement, and control [69]. This capability improves sensing efficiency and guides sensor placement toward informative regions. This work develops the mathematical and algorithmic foundations for such an integrated system, focusing on source identification problems in which the digital twin directly informs sensor placement. This is of particular interest given rapid advances in neural digital twins where model inference is feasible on lightweight hardware [36].

We consider the optimal coverage problem for source identification, where mobile sensors must arrange themselves to identify the location of an unknown source term. Such problems involve sparse, indirect, and noisy observations of the transported field. Accurate reconstruction requires inverting the transport process, which is generally ill-posed. Traditional methods rely on prior knowledge, typically the exact form of the transport dynamics, the geometry, and possible source configurations [8]. Because transport dynamics smooth and displace the influence of the source, the inverse problem is often highly ill-posed and sensitive to observation quality [28]. In many real-world settings, dense sensing is infeasible, and the ability to adaptively allocate limited mobile sensors is essential for accurate estimation [34, 46]. Mobile sensors provide a cost-efficient and adaptable means of data collection in dynamic or unknown environments; for example, in the Earth’s oceans, where it is infeasible to establish a dense network of seafaring drones.

Classical inverse methods, such as variational formulations and PDE-constrained optimization, provide principled tools for source reconstruction, but they typically assume full-field measurements, detailed knowledge of the underlying system, and require handcrafted regularization to mitigate ill-posedness [20]. More recently, data-driven and machine learning approaches have emerged as flexible alternatives, using neural networks to approximate forward or inverse maps directly from partial observations [6]. However, such models often lack interpretable parameterization (i.e., are treated as black boxes) [57, 42], or impose governing equations only as soft constraints, leading to violations of physical consistency [63]. In inverse settings, this can yield implausible reconstructions, poor generalization under sparse data, and limited interpretability, posing challenges for high-consequence applications. Moreover, most machine-learned surrogates are not easily integrated with adaptive sampling or real-time feedback, limiting their use in adaptive sensing tasks.

We propose a structure-preserving framework for inverse source identification that directly embeds the conservation laws of the governing equations into a learned surrogate PDE model, without assuming a fixed functional form. Rather than learning the inverse operator, we learn both the source term and a nonlinear flux describing the transport process on a reduced finite element basis, and reconstruct the scalar field by solving the coupled conservation equation. We employ the recently proposed Conditional Neural Whitney Forms method (CNWF) [36]. All fields are discretized using finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) [5, 4], ensuring compatibility with geometry and exact discrete conservation [1, 63]. The source is represented as a normalized spatial density over a reduced partition-of-unity basis, yielding interpretable estimates compliant with conservation structure. This formulation explicitly couples the observed scalar field and the unknown source through a shared PDE constraint that regularizes the inverse problem and preserves physical structure throughout inference.

Recent transformer-based operator learning approaches lack explicit physical structure, relying instead on their powerful approximation properties to achieve accurate predictions. Our method integrates a transformer encoder into a finite element framework, combining the flexibility of attention-based models with the guarantees of FEEC. Conditioning enables the pretrained PDE operator to adapt in real time to sensor data, similar to how generative computer vision models sample images from a distribution conditioned on a text prompt. We supervise on both the scalar field and source term over training datasets to ensure consistency with the governing PDE, while downstream tasks use only the learned source term. An overview is given in Figure 1 and explained in detail in Section 5.1. A deep explanation of the FEEC framework is beyond the scope of this paper, and we direct interested readers to [36].

To enable a closed-loop connection between inference and sensing, we interpret the learned source field as an importance distribution that guides sensor placement via a geodesic implementation of Lloyd’s algorithm [43] for nonconvex domains. This yields a two-scale optimization scheme: at each outer iteration, sensors are repositioned to minimize expected distance under the predicted importance field, and the model is updated with new observations from the new sensor locations. We provide a theoretical basis establishing improvements in prediction accuracy, model-relative coverage, and true coverage objectives under suitable regularity and accuracy conditions. This defines a closed feedback loop in which improved sensing leads to better predictions, which in turn guide sensors toward more informative configurations.

We validate our method on prototypical passive scalar transport systems. In all cases, our approach outperforms standard baselines, including an identical transformer model lacking structure preservation. We show that the proposed model improves both the inverse problem and yields even larger relative gains when coupled with adaptive sampling. The resulting predictions are more consistent with the governing PDE. Physical structure, reduced-basis interpretability, and integrated mobile sensor control together enable accurate source recovery under sparse and noisy data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining structure-preserving modeling with adaptive sampling for inverse problems in transport-dominated systems.

3 Problem statement

We study inverse source identification problems governed by steady-state advection–diffusion physics on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with a given divergence-free velocity field and Péclet number. The scalar field u:Ω→ℝu:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} satisfies the forward model used in experiments,

−1Pe​∇2u+𝐯⋅∇u=fin ​Ω,u|∂Ω=g,-\frac{1}{\text{Pe}}\nabla^{2}u+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla u=f\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad u|_{\partial\Omega}=g, (6)

where Pe>0\text{Pe}>0 is the Péclet number, 𝐯:Ω→ℝd\mathbf{v}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is an unknown, divergence-free velocity field scaled so that ‖𝐯‖L∞​(Ω)=1\|\mathbf{v}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=1, gg is a fixed boundary condition, and f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is an unknown source field.

We assume access to a set of NN mobile sensors at locations X={𝐱i}i=1NX=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, each recording local measurements of the scalar and velocity fields, along with the global Péclet number:

zi=(𝐱i,u⁡(𝐱i)+ηi(u),𝐯⁡(𝐱i)+ηi(v),Pe),z_{i}=\left(\mathbf{x}_{i},\;u(\mathbf{x}_{i})+\eta_{i}^{(u)},\;\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_{i})+\eta_{i}^{(v)},\text{Pe}\right), (7)

where ηi(u)\eta_{i}^{(u)}, ηi(v)\eta_{i}^{(v)} are independent additive noise terms. We aim to infer the unknown source field ff from these noisy, sparse observations, and to guide sensor placement toward regions that improve reconstruction quality [62].

In this work we must solve two subproblems (SP1-2):

SP1 Source identification: Given sparse, local observations z={zi}z=\{z_{i}\}, estimate a normalized source density ρθ(⋅∣z)\rho_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z) from a parameterized model, such that the corresponding scalar field u~θ\tilde{u}_{\theta}, obtained by solving (6) with learned source fθf_{\theta}, matches the supervising field and source data. SP2 Adaptive sensor placement: Use the predicted density ρθ(⋅∣z)\rho_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z) as an importance function to adaptively steer the sensor positions XX by minimizing the coverage energy functional: 𝒥⁡(X)=∫Ωρθ​(𝐱∣z)​min1≤i≤N⁡g⁡(d⁡(𝐱,𝐱i))​𝑑𝐱,\mathcal{J}(X)=\int_{\Omega}\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\mid z)\,\min_{1\leq i\leq N}g(d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{i}))\,d\mathbf{x}, (8) where d⁡(𝐱,𝐲)d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is a distance metric on the domain and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) is a non-decreasing function describing sensor degradation [14].

In concert, these form a closed-loop inference-and-control problem: we alternate between estimating the source from current observations and repositioning sensors to improve future inference. The remainder of the paper develops a structure-preserving surrogate model that drives this loop, along with an implementation of a geodesic Lloyd algorithm [43, 14] for sensor coverage optimization. We demonstrate the combination for an adaptive sensor-placement algorithm for source localization with supporting analysis and empirical convergence to the true source location and improvement over baseline models without structure preservation.

4 Prior work

4.1 Inverse source identification in PDEs

Classical approaches to source identification in transport systems formulate the problem as a PDE-constrained optimization task, typically regularized via Tikhonov penalties and solved using adjoint-state or iterative methods [11, 7]. These approaches offer interpretability and explicit control over regularization and error metrics, but they can degrade under sparse/noisy observations and require repeated PDE solves, which is challenging for mobile or real-time sensing. Alternative strategies based on Bayesian inversion [62, 61] and model-based data assimilation [3] have been developed to mitigate these limitations.

4.2 Sensor placement and source-seeking strategies

When sensing is expensive or constrained, accurate inversion depends not only on the quality of the model but on data collection itself [48, 68]. In robotics and environmental monitoring, heuristic strategies like chemotaxis [58, 47], infotaxis, and entropy maximization have long been used for source localization [58, 67, 18, 71, 60]. Gaussian Process models provide a principled Bayesian approach and can be integrated with prior physical data [34]. Complementing these are coverage-based methods such as Lloyd’s algorithm and its generalizations, which provide a principled approach by minimizing the coverage cost in (8) [24, 25].

4.3 Data-driven inverse modeling

Machine learning methods have emerged as a flexible alternative for solving inverse problems under sparse and noisy data, or in uncertain settings [16, 49, 31, 64, 38, 55]. Operator learning methods, such as DeepONets and Fourier neural operators, attempt to learn mappings between function spaces directly [41, 45], and can be used for inverse problems where the input is the solution space [51]. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) incorporate differential constraints into the loss function [54] and have been widely explored for inverse problems [70, 29]. Broadly, physical structure is imposed weakly if at all, and the coupling between the sampled field and the source term of interest must be implicitly deduced from training [32, 65, 10]. The resulting models can be unstable or uninterpretable [66, 30].

4.4 Structure-preserving learning

A promising direction in machine learning is the development of structure-preserving machine learning strategies which incorporate physical or geometric structure either by construction of neural architechtures or by training with hard constraints, enforcing e.g: symmetries, conservation laws, or geometric invariants [22, 13, 9, 12, 26, 53]. We consider methods grounded in geometric discretization, where structure preservation is enforced through differential form-based representations of physical quantities through Finite Element Exterior Calculus (FEEC) [5].

Discrete Exterior Calculus (DEC) and Finite Element Exterior Calculus (FEEC) provide tools for discretizations with exact discrete preservation of topological identities (e.g., Stokes/Gauss), flux balances, and cohomology classes [4, 17]. Whitney forms, in particular, define basis functions that represent fields, fluxes, and sources in conforming mixed finite element spaces that interpolate corresponding differential forms, inheriting in the process exact treatment of the generalized Stokes theorems [44]. These foundations have been extended to machine learning, with recent methods incorporating data-driven Whitney forms, learned partitions of unity, and graph-based exterior calculus into neural architectures [63, 1, 30]. The resulting models offer conservation by design, interpretable structure, and principled integration with mesh-based physical domains, making them especially well-suited to inverse problems where both the source and its observational effects are governed by conservation laws.

5 Methodology

5.1 Learnable structure-preserving reduced order model

We summarize the approach developed in [36] here, but defer to the previous work for details. Our contribution at the ROM level is the introduction of a conditional source field, in addition to the conditional shape functions and physics considered in the original work.

The original governing equations (6) hold at the differential level; however, after an aggressive dimension reduction, we assume that only the conservation structure holds

∇⋅𝐅⁡(u)=fin ​Ω,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}(u)=f\quad\text{in }\Omega, (9)

where 𝐅\mathbf{F} is a conserved flux and ff is a scalar source field; the fluxes encoded by 𝐅\mathbf{F} are assumed to contain the effective homogenization of the physics onto a reduced basis and therefore differ from the original model. In the data-driven FEEC framework [36, 1, 63], the unknown fluxes are posed as a Lipschitz nonlinearity (potentially conditioned on zz) stabilized by a diffusive flux,

𝐅θ(u,z)=−ε∇u+𝒩θ(u,z),\mathbf{F}_{\theta}(u,z)=-\varepsilon\nabla u+\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(u,z), (10)

for some trainable ε>0\varepsilon>0. Discretizing with a mixed Galerkin setting taking uu and 𝐅\mathbf{F} as Whitney forms, we obtain a discrete nonlinear model encoding the conservation relationships. Identifying the mass matrices of Whitney forms with the Hodge star in the Discrete Exterior Calculus (DEC), we can interpret the flux as a parameterized co-chain to co-chain map between degrees of freedom for uu and 𝐅\mathbf{F}; put plainly, the Whitney forms describing uu and 𝐅\mathbf{F} model geometry associated with control volumes and their areas, respectively, while 𝒩\mathcal{N} models the exchange of conserved quantities between them.

This approach offers particular advantages over black box techniques:

  • •

    It incorporates complex geometry directly through the finite element bilinear forms, avoiding issues encountered by popular neural operators on non-trivial domains.

  • •

    It guarantees exact conservation of flux–source balance at the discrete level by construction so that predictions satisfy conservation principles independent of data sparsity.

  • •

    The model admits a Lax-Milgram-style stability theory, with a consequent well-posedness theorem (See [36, Thm. 2.1], [63, Thms. 3.1-5]) that guarantees existence of weak solution even when the model is solved out of distribution. This imposes an inductive bias toward regular, physically-meaningful solutions in data sparse regimes.

  • •

    It explicitly couples the source prediction to the learned flux through the local conservation principle (See e.g.[63, Sec. 3]), exposing an exploitable linkage between local sensor readings of the field/flux state and the global location and magnitude of sources.

By conditioning 𝒩\mathcal{N} and ff on sensor readings, we obtain a parametric discrete model which specializes to sensor data through the conditioning variable zz; after denoting discrete operators with a superscript hh, we express the model as

−ε​Δh​u+∇h⋅𝒩θh​(u,z)=𝒮θh​(z)in ​Ω,u|∂Ω=g.-\varepsilon\Delta^{h}u+\nabla^{h}\cdot\mathcal{N}^{h}_{\theta}(u,z)=\mathcal{S}^{h}_{\theta}(z)\quad\text{in }\Omega,\quad u|_{\partial\Omega}=g. (11)

Further details on the discrete system may be found in Section 5.2. While the conditioning of digital twins through trainable Whitney forms and fluxes was first described in [36], the current work introduces the learned source term 𝒮θ​(z)\mathcal{S}_{\theta}(z), which is crucial for the task of source identification. After performing the conditioning step in SP1, the learned 𝒮θh​(z)\mathcal{S}^{h}_{\theta}(z) is then used to construct the importance function ρθ​(𝐱∣z)\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\mid z) in SP2.

5.2 Discretization

We summarize the discretization process here, referring readers to Trask et al. [63] for a detailed description of data-driven Whitney forms and Kinch et al. [36] for further details of the conditioning transformer and problem setup.

The scalar field uu and source ff are identified as 0-forms, while the flux 𝐅\mathbf{F} is identified as a 1-form; both are expanded in low order Whitney forms of the corresponding degree (specifically, 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and Nedelec elements) on a simplicial mesh of Ω\Omega. Let {φi0}i=1n0f\{\varphi_{i}^{0}\}_{i=1}^{n_{0}^{f}} denote the 0-form basis with nodal degrees of freedom, and {φe1}e=1n1f\{\varphi_{e}^{1}\}_{e=1}^{n_{1}^{f}} the 1-forms with tangential edge degrees of freedom.

To reduce computational cost and allow for adaptive resolution, we construct a data-dependent reduced basis for 0-forms. Specifically, we define coarse scalar basis functions {ψj0}j=1n0c⊂H1​(Ω)\{\psi_{j}^{0}\}_{j=1}^{n_{0}^{c}}\subset H^{1}(\Omega) as convex combinations of the fine-scale basis:

ψj0​(x)=∑i=1n0fWj​i​(z)​φi0​(x),\psi_{j}^{0}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{0}^{f}}W_{ji}(z)\,\varphi_{i}^{0}(x), (12)

where W⁡(z)∈ℝn0c×n0fW(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}^{c}\times n_{0}^{f}} is a learned, nonnegative matrix with:

Wj​i≥0,∑j=1n0cWj​i=1for all i.W_{ji}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{n_{0}^{c}}W_{ji}=1\quad\text{for all }i. (13)

This construction ensures that {ψj0}\{\psi_{j}^{0}\} forms a partition of unity over Ω\Omega, and defines a set of interpretable control volumes. This exposes a fully connected graph structure, with the learned fluxes operating on the edges. In practice this basis may be of order 1-10 elements, drastically compressing the original 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} basis.

Following the standard FEEC construction, coarsened 1-forms must be constructed which support a surjective coboundary operator. We do this by applying the standard construction of Nedelec elements to the coarsened basis.

ψ1i​j=ψ0j∇ψ0i−ψ0i∇ψ0j,\psi^{1}_{ij}=\psi^{0}_{j}\nabla\psi^{0}_{i}-\psi^{0}_{i}\nabla\psi^{0}_{j}, (14)

defining subspaces of the original de Rham complex which form a de Rham complex of their own. The current work requires only the d​i​v−g​r​a​ddiv-grad subcomplex; see [1] for details of the complete complex.

All quantities are represented on this reduced basis without loss of structure. The reduced scalar field coefficients u^∈ℝn0c\hat{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}^{c}}, fluxes 𝐅^∈ℝn1c\hat{\mathbf{F}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}^{c}}, and sources f^∈ℝn0c\hat{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}^{c}} are defined in terms of coarse Whitney forms {ψj0},{ψi​j1}\{\psi_{j}^{0}\},\{\psi_{ij}^{1}\}. We may easily pull back the coarsened Whitney forms onto the fine scale mesh through the affine operations fθ=W⊤​f^θf_{\theta}=W^{\top}\hat{f}_{\theta}, and uθ=W⊤​u^θu_{\theta}=W^{\top}\hat{u}_{\theta}.

The discrete conservation law is expressed in the reduced basis as:

ε​δ0⊤​M1​δ0​u^+δ0⊤​M1​𝒩θ​(u^,z)⏟ℱ⁡(u^,θ,z)=M0​f^θ​(z)⏟b⁡(θ,z),\underbrace{\varepsilon\delta_{0}^{\top}M_{1}\delta_{0}\hat{u}+\delta_{0}^{\top}M_{1}\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\hat{u},z)}_{\mathcal{F}(\hat{u};\theta,z)}=\underbrace{M_{0}\hat{f}_{\theta}(z)}_{b(\theta,z)}, (15)

where M0,M1M_{0},M_{1} are reduced mass matrices for the coarsened 0- and 1- forms, respectively, and δ0\delta_{0} is the reduced coboundary operator. This yields the PDE constraint,

H⁡(u^,θ,z):=ℱ⁡(u^,θ,z)−b⁡(θ,z)=0.H(\hat{u};\theta,z):=\mathcal{F}(\hat{u};\theta,z)-b(\theta,z)=0. (16)

See [36, 63] for details of matrix assembly and solver setup.

5.3 Learnable parameterization

We parameterize the source, flux, and basis networks in (15) as task-specific heads built on a shared transformer encoder, ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta}. The encoder maps the unordered sensor inputs to a latent representation, which conditions each component of the surrogate PDE model (adaptive basis, flux, and source). The implementation is based on the cross-attention transformer CNWF method proposed in [36], with modifications to accommodate the adaptive sensing and source identification application. Full architectural details are given in Appendix Appendix A: Neural Network Parameterization Details.

5.4 Source identification

In the source identification problem, we seek to recover the unobserved source field responsible for generating sparse and noisy observations of the scalar field uu, under the governing PDE (advection-diffusion in our experiments). We assume access to a set of NN sensors distributed across the domain Ω\Omega, which make point measurements to form the model conditioning input, z={zi}i=1Nz=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}.

Notably, the underlying source field ff is unobserved. Recovering it from indirect field measurements requires solving an ill-posed inverse problem, where physical constraints are essential for meaningful inference.

The predicted source fθ​(z)f_{\theta}(z) is normalized to integrate to one (after projection onto φ0\varphi^{0}), with nonegativity enforced (e.g. via ReLU),

ρθ​(𝐱|z)=fθ​(z)​(𝐱)∫Ωfθ​(z)​(𝐲)​𝑑𝐲,ρθ≥0,∫Ωρθ=1,\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\,|\,z)\;=\;\frac{f_{\theta}(z)(\mathbf{x})}{\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}f_{\theta}(z)(\mathbf{y})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}},\qquad\rho_{\theta}\geq 0,\;\int_{\Omega}\rho_{\theta}=1, (17)

so that ρθ\rho_{\theta} may be interpreted as a spatial probability density for the point-source location, or source distribution in complex source cases.

To train the model, we solve the PDE-constrained optimization problem for a given normalized source term ρtrue\rho_{\mathrm{true}} and the corresponding solution utrueu_{\mathrm{true}} as:

minθ\displaystyle\min_{\theta}\; ∥uθ(θ,z)−utrue∥2+W2,ϵ2(ρtrue,ρθ(⋅|z))\displaystyle\|u_{\theta}(\theta,z)-u_{\text{true}}\|^{2}+W_{2,\epsilon}^{2}(\rho_{\mathrm{true}},\rho_{\theta}(\,\cdot\,|\,z)) (18)
subject toH⁡(uθ,θ,z)=0,\displaystyle\text{subject to}\quad H(u_{\theta},\theta,z)=0, (19)

where W2,ϵ2W_{2,\epsilon}^{2} corresponds to the 2-Wasserstein distance as an optimal transport metric for the source reconstruction; due to the compact nature of the source, a simple MSE objective performed poorly. We approximately compute the geodesic Wasserstein metric using the sinkhorn distance [15].

  • •

    Following the well-posedness of Equation 15, 18 has a non-empty feasible set, and thus any solution satisfies Equation 15.

  • •

    Consequently, the learned model enforces topological structure independent of data availability, optimizer error, or extant of extrapolation.

See [36] for details on the solution of the constrained optimization problem.

5.5 Adaptive source localization

Given the model-defined source distribution ρθ\rho_{\theta}, we implement the classic Lloyd’s algorithm for optimal coverage to distribute sensors within the domain [14]. We describe a geodesic implementation to allow generalization to complex, non-convex geometries, as shown in the results. Lloyd’s algorithm arises from quantization and, in the Euclidean setting, provides monotonic descent towards a weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation (CVT) [19], which is known to minimize the coverage functional (e.g. (8)), and therefore has been adapted in distributed sensor placement [14]. For all computations we rely on a discretized approximation on the original mesh, allowing for accurate evaluation of integrals with quadrature and computational efficiency.

We start by defining the geodesic distance inside the possibly non-convex domain Ω\Omega by dΩ​(𝐱,𝐲)d_{\Omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),

dΩ​(𝐱,𝐲)=infγ∈C1​([0,1],Ω¯)γ⁡(0)=𝐱,γ⁡(1)=𝐲∫01‖γ′​(t)‖​𝑑t,d_{\Omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in C^{1}\!\bigl([0,1],\overline{\Omega}\bigr)\\ \gamma(0)=\mathbf{x},\,\gamma(1)=\mathbf{y}\end{subarray}}\int_{0}^{1}\!\bigl\|\gamma^{\prime}(t)\bigr\|\,\mathrm{d}t,

i.e. the length of the shortest C1C^{1} path contained in Ω¯\overline{\Omega} that joins the points 𝐱,𝐲∈Ω¯\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\overline{\Omega}, where Ω¯=Ω∪∂Ω\overline{\Omega}=\Omega\cup\partial\Omega [35]. Let

Vi(𝐗)={𝐱∈Ω:dΩ(𝐱,𝐱i)≤dΩ(𝐱,𝐱j),j≠i}V_{i}(\mathbf{X})=\bigl\{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega:\,d_{\Omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{i})\leq d_{\Omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{j}),\;j\neq i\bigr\}

denote the geodesic Voronoi cell for a generator xix_{i}.

By selecting the sensor positions {xi}\{x_{i}\} as the Voronoi generators and using the geodesic distance function and g⁡(x):=x2g(x):=x^{2}, the localization objective (8) is:

𝒥⁡(𝐗)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\mathbf{X}) =∑i=1N∫Vi​(𝐗)ρ⁡(𝐪)​dΩ2​(𝐪,𝐱i)​𝑑𝐪,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\int_{V_{i}(\mathbf{X})}\rho(\mathbf{q})d_{\Omega}^{2}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x}_{i})\mathrm{d}\mathbf{q}, (20)

i.e., the expected squared geodesic distance from a random point within the domain to the nearest sensor, weighted by the importance, ρ\rho.

In the original paper [14], ρ⁡(𝐪)\rho(\mathbf{q}) is an a priori specified field, typically empirically via heuristics. In contrast, for the current work ρ\rho is prescribed via 𝒮θh​(z)\mathcal{S}^{h}_{\theta}(z) so that the localization objective weight is constrained to satisfy a physics-based PDE. Unlike the original work, ρ\rho is now an implicit function of the sensor locations, and so the original analysis in [14] no longer holds. We present analysis following from this modification in Sections 5.6, 5.7, and 5.8.

The aim of our sensor placement approach is to minimize (20) over a given, unknown source term ρtrue\rho_{\mathrm{true}}. In the case of a single event as the source term with a probability distribution ρt​r​u​e\rho_{true}, the localization objective corresponds to maximizing the observation probability over the domain for sensors whose sensing capabilities degrade (e.g. due to noise) as dΩ​(⋅)2d_{\Omega}(\cdot)^{2}. When ρ\rho corresponds to the location of an emitter, this can be viewed as improving the observability of the source, and therefore is expected to improve the conditioning of the inverse problem.

To update the sensor locations in the conventional Lloyd’s implementation we define a gradient flow towards the centroid, cic_{i}, with a relaxation α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1],

x˙i=−α⁡(xi−ci).\dot{x}_{i}=-\alpha(x_{i}-c_{i}). (21)

To modify this for discrete updates the nonconvex setting and enable coverage on complex geometries, we consider the generalized geodesic path, γ\gamma, between the sensor and the centroid. We define the update as

𝐱i(k+1):=γ𝐱ik→𝐜ik(k)​(α),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(k+1)}:=\gamma_{\mathbf{x}^{k}_{i}\to\mathbf{c}^{k}_{i}}^{(k)}(\alpha), (22)

i.e. a movement along the geodesic path proportional to α\alpha. This reduces to (21) in the convex setting. This formulation preserves feasibility by construction since γi(k)​(t)∈Vi⊂Ω\gamma_{i}^{(k)}(t)\in V_{i}\subset\Omega for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], and provides a tunable tradeoff between convergence speed and robustness in the presence of uncertainty. In practice, the path γi(k)\gamma_{i}^{(k)} is discretized using fast marching and interpolated using geodesic barycentric coordinates on the mesh.

The geodesic centroid of a Voronoi region Vi⊂ΩV_{i}\subset\Omega is defined as the intrinsic mean:

𝐜i=arg⁡min⁡∫Vi𝐲∈Ω⁡dΩ​(𝐲,𝐱)2​ρθ​(𝐱)​𝑑𝐱,\mathbf{c}_{i}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\Omega}\int_{V_{i}}d_{\Omega}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})^{2}\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}, (23)

which is guaranteed to be unique on Hadamard manifolds [2]. In Euclidean space, this reduces to the standard centroid:

𝐜i=1Mi​∫Vi𝐱​ρθ​(𝐱)​𝑑𝐱,Mi=∫Viρθ​(𝐱)​𝑑𝐱.\mathbf{c}_{i}=\frac{1}{M_{i}}\int_{V_{i}}\mathbf{x}\,\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x},\quad M_{i}=\int_{V_{i}}\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}.

Since computing (23) is expensive, we approximate it by computing the Euclidean centroid c¯i\bar{c}_{i} and projecting it into the geodesic Voronoi cell if it lies outside the region:

𝐜i:=arg⁡min𝐱∈Vi⁡‖𝐱−𝐜¯i‖22.\mathbf{c}_{i}:=\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in V_{i}}\;\|\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{c}}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. (24)

This ensures feasibility and, in convex geometries, reproduces the classic Lloyd update. Algorithm 1 describes the discrete, geodesic Lloyd algorithm for a given set of sensor locations and a density. Geodesic distances are computed using the exact discrete geodesic algorithm of Mitchell–Mount–Papadimitriou as implemented in pygeodesic [50]; integrals are evaluated by quadrature over the mesh.

5.6 Convergence of source localization algorithms

We now examine the convergence of Lloyd’s update rule when the importance field varies externally over time. Lloyd’s algorithm is known to produce a monotonic energy descent of the coverage functional for a convex geometry with a fixed importance, guaranteeing convergence to a CVT [14]. We must consider the more complex setting where the importance density is a time varying function of the sensor locations, as is the case in our application. We establish a sufficient condition under which convergence is preserved despite variations.

We define the Lloyd update rule for a set of generator positions xkx_{k} and importance field ρk\rho_{k} as G⁡(xk,ρk)=:xk+1G(x_{k},\rho_{k})=:x_{k+1}, and note that in this general setting the algorithm implemented in GG can be mm steps of the the discrete Lloyd described in Algorithm 1, or some time integration in a continuous implementation. We consider the corresponding set of importance updates {ρk}k=1K\{\rho_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} coming from a model ρk+1:=ρθ​(xk)\rho_{k+1}:=\rho_{\theta}(x_{k}) with an initial estimate ρ0\rho_{0}, and the resulting set generator positions be {xk={x1k,…,xnk}}k=1K\{x_{k}=\{x_{1}^{k},\ldots,x_{n}^{k}\}\}_{k=1}^{K}. Let 𝒥ρ​(x)\mathcal{J}_{\rho}(x) denote the coverage energy functional with importance ρ\rho and generator locations xx.

We assume throughout this section that the current sensor configuration xkx_{k} is suboptimal with respect to the current importance field ρk\rho_{k} (i.e., not a centroidal Voronoi configuration). This ensures that the Lloyd update yields strict energy descent. We define the strictly decreasing change in the coverage energy 𝒥\mathcal{J} due to the Lloyd update as:

Δ​𝒥kLloyd:=𝒥ρk​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk)<0,\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}:=\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})<0,

additionally we define the change in the coverage energy due to the model update

Δ​𝒥kmodel:=𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk+1).\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}:=\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1}).
Theorem 1 (Monotonic decrease of model-relative coverage).

We consider the general setting with no assumption of the dependence of ρk\rho_{k} on xkx_{k} for this theorem. If the importance update satisfies

‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞<−Δ​𝒥kLloydCΩ,\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\frac{-\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}}{C_{\Omega}},

for some constant CΩ>0C_{\Omega}>0 depending only on the domain geometry, then the combined two-step update satisfies

𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)<𝒥ρk​(xk),\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})<\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k}),

and the model-relative coverage energy is strictly decreasing.

Proof.

The total energy change across one iteration is:

𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k}) =𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk+1)+𝒥ρk​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk)\displaystyle=\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1})+\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})
=Δ​𝒥kmodel+Δ​𝒥kLloyd.\displaystyle=\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}+\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}.

To bound the model update term Δ​𝒥kmodel\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}, we use the linearity of 𝒥\mathcal{J} in ρ\rho:

|Δ​𝒥kmodel|\displaystyle|\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}| =|∑i=1n∫Vi​(xk+1)(ρk+1​(q)−ρk​(q))​dΩ​(q,xik+1)2​𝑑q|\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{V_{i}(x_{k+1})}\left(\rho_{k+1}(q)-\rho_{k}(q)\right)d_{\Omega}(q,x_{i}^{k+1})^{2}\,dq\right|
≤‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞​∑i=1n∫Vi​(xk+1)dΩ​(q,xik+1)2​𝑑q.\displaystyle\leq\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{V_{i}(x_{k+1})}d_{\Omega}(q,x_{i}^{k+1})^{2}\,dq.

Define the geometry-dependent constant

CΩ:=supx∈Ωn∑i=1n∫Vi​(x)dΩ​(q,xi)2​𝑑q,C_{\Omega}:=\sup_{x\in\Omega^{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{V_{i}(x)}d_{\Omega}(q,x_{i})^{2}\,dq,

which is finite on Ω\Omega with bounded diameter. Then,

Δ​𝒥kmodel≤|Δ​𝒥kmodel|≤CΩ​‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞.\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}\leq|\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{model}}|\leq C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Combining the two terms, the total energy change satisfies:

𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk)≤CΩ​‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞+Δ​𝒥kLloyd.\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})\leq C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}.

By the assumption of the theorem, we have:

‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞<−Δ​𝒥kLloydCΩ,\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\frac{-\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}}{C_{\Omega}},

which implies that the right-hand side is strictly negative due to the strict Lloyd energy descent. Therefore,

𝒥ρk+1​(xk+1)<𝒥ρk​(xk),\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k+1}}(x_{k+1})<\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k}),

and the model-relative coverage energy is strictly decreasing.

Remark 1

We view Δ​JLloyd\Delta J^{\mathrm{Lloyd}} as a buffer which increases the tolerance to changes in the importance density, ρ\rho. The isolation of the sensor movement from the importance updates gives an elegant opportunity to control this buffer by simply increasing the number of inner Lloyd steps taken. For a given proposed importance update ρn​e​w\rho_{new} we can guarantee the condition in (1) to be satisfied by increasing mm, so long as the sub-optimality of the initial configuration is greater than the change in energy due to the importance update, i.e.

‖ρk+1−ρk‖L∞<𝒥ρk​(xk)−𝒥ρk​(x∗)CΩ,\|\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\frac{\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x^{*})}{C_{\Omega}},

where x∗x^{*} are the optimal generator positions, x∗:=argminx​𝒥ρk​(x)x^{*}:=\text{argmin}_{x}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x).

Remark 2

We note that we can alternatively ensure the regularity of the importance updates and therefore guarantee Theorem 1 is satisfied if we employ an optimized convex update to the importance field given a candidate update ρnew\rho_{\mathrm{new}} as:

ρk+1=α​ρk+(1−α)​ρnew\rho_{k+1}=\alpha\rho_{k}+(1-\alpha)\rho_{\mathrm{new}}

for

α=inf{α′∈[0,1]|ρk+1​satisfies (1)}.\alpha=\inf\left\{\alpha^{\prime}\in[0,1]|\;\rho_{k+1}\;\text{satisfies \eqref{eq:theorem1_condition}}\right\}.

This provides a guaranteed valid update in all ρnew\rho_{\mathrm{new}} for α=0⟹‖ρk+1−ρk‖=0\alpha=0\implies\left\lVert\rho_{k+1}-\rho_{k}\right\rVert=0.

5.7 Model driven importance updates

We now consider the case where the importance field is a function of the sensor locations, as in our application, where ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) is parameterized with the CNWF source network on the learned basis functions.

Theorem 2 (Monotonic decrease of true coverage objective).

Let: ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) be a map from sensor positions to an estimated importance field, 𝒥ρ​(x)\mathcal{J}_{\rho}(x) denote the model-relative coverage functional, and 𝒥ρtrue​(x)\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x) be the true coverage functional. Recall from Theorem 1 that 𝒥\mathcal{J} is Lipschitz in ρ\rho with constant CΩC_{\Omega}.

If the condition

Δ​𝒥kLloyd<−2​CΩ​‖ρ⁡(xk)−ρtrue‖∞\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}<-2C_{\Omega}\|\rho(x_{k})-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}

is satisfied, and the generator position updates follow a Lloyd descent, then the true coverage energy strictly decreases:

𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<𝒥ρtrue​(xk).\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}).

Proof.

We decompose the change in true coverage energy into model errors at steps kk, k+1k+1 and the descent step:

Δ​𝒥k=\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}= 𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)−𝒥ρtrue​(xk)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k})
=\displaystyle= [𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk+1)]+Δ​𝒥kLloyd+[𝒥ρk​(xk)−𝒥ρtrue​(xk)].\displaystyle\left[\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1})\right]+\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}+\left[\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k})\right].

Applying the Lipschitz continuity in ρ\rho:

|𝒥ρtrue​(xk)−𝒥ρk​(xk)|≤CΩ​‖ρk−ρtrue‖∞,|\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k})|\leq C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty},
|𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)−𝒥ρk​(xk+1)|≤CΩ​‖ρk−ρtrue‖∞.|\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}}(x_{k+1})|\leq C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}.

Thus

𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)−𝒥ρtrue​(xk)≤Δ​𝒥kLloyd+2​CΩ​‖ρk−ρtrue‖∞.\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})-\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k})\leq\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{\mathrm{Lloyd}}+2C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}.

If the condition in the theorem is satisfied and the combined prediction error is small relative to the Lloyd’s descent energy change,

2​CΩ​‖ρk−ρtrue‖∞<Δ​𝒥kL​l​o​y​d,2C_{\Omega}\|\rho_{k}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}<\Delta\mathcal{J}_{k}^{Lloyd},

then

𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<𝒥ρtrue​(xk),\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}),

and thus we achieve strict decrease in the true coverage energy.

Theorem 3.

(Monotonic decrease in prediction error bound) If the generator updates provide a strict decrease in the coverage energy (e.g., if Theorem 2 is satisfied),

𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<𝒥ρtrue​(xk),\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}),

and we additionally assume that the prediction error is bounded by a positive constant multiple of the true coverage energy, CΦC_{\Phi}, such that,

‖ρ⁡(xk)−ρtrue‖∞≤CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk).\|\rho(x_{k})-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}).

It follows that the model prediction error bound is strictly decreasing,

‖ρ⁡(xk+1)−ρtrue‖≤CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk).\|\rho(x_{k+1})-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|\leq C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}).

Proof.

Assume there exists a constant CΦ>0C_{\Phi}>0, such that for all xx,

‖ρ⁡(x)−ρtrue‖≤CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(x).\|\rho(x)-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|\leq C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x).

Under the strict energy decrease in Theorem 2,

CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk),C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}),

and therefore

‖ρ⁡(xk+1)−ρtrue‖∞≤CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk+1)<CΦ​𝒥ρtrue​(xk).\|\rho(x_{k+1})-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k+1})<C_{\Phi}\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{\mathrm{true}}}(x_{k}).

Remark 3

We interpret the constant CΦC_{\Phi} as a relation between the informativeness of the sensor configuration, and the well-posedness of the inverse problem. For a sufficiently well-trained model, we expect this to correspond to improved predictions, or a reduced error bound. We note that this condition is dependent on model training and construction and cannot generally be guaranteed.

We conclude that if Theorems 1, 2, and 3 are satisfied, reducing the model-relative coverage energy results in both a reduction in the true coverage energy, and a strict improvement in model prediction error bound. This establishes a positive feedback loop for the true coverage objective, where improvements in sensor positioning result in improved prediction error bounds, which may in turn result in improved sensor placement relative to the true coverage goal, provided the error bound, CΦC_{\Phi}, is sufficiently tight, which can be verified empirically.

In order for these to be satisfied we require that the importance updates satisfy a regularity condition over iterations, that the importance predictions satisfy an accuracy condition compared to the true field, and that the true coverage energy can be used to bound the prediction error. As described in Remark 5.6, the regularity condition can be satisfied by construction, but the other conditions are dependent on model training and can not be easily guaranteed in practical settings, so we rely on empirical confirmation of the convergence of the prediction error, model-relative coverage, and true coverage energies to validate these assumptions are approximately satisfied in our experimental setting.

5.8 Convergence to source location

While the previous analysis established that coverage control with model updates can reduce the coverage cost, we now address the stronger property of convergence of a sensor to the true source location. We study a simplified but representative setting in which the source is a Dirac delta at x∗x^{*} and the learned model produces a smooth bump function centered near x∗x^{*} with a uniform background value, sharpening towards a Dirac as the nearest sensor approaches the source location. In this setting, we show that under continuous Lloyd dynamics the minimal distance between sensors and the source converges to zero exponentially fast, thereby closing the gap between coverage minimization and source convergence.

Theorem 4.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a convex domain equipped with the Euclidean distance. Let x∗∈Ωx^{*}\in\Omega denote the true source location and

m⁡(t):=mini⁡‖xi​(t)−x∗‖m(t):=\min_{i}\|x_{i}(t)-x^{*}\|

the minimal distance from any sensor xix_{i} to x∗x^{*}. Suppose the learned importance function ρθ(⋅∣z)\rho_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z) satisfies two conditions:

  1. 1.

    If m⁡(X)=0m(X)=0, then ρ⁡(X)=δ⁡(x∗)\rho(X)=\delta(x^{*}).

  2. 2.

    Centroids vary in a locally Lipschitz continuous manner that is contractive, meaning that there exists a critical distance mc>0m_{\mathrm{c}}>0 and r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) such that for all configurations X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} with respective minimal distances m1,m2<mcm_{1},m_{2}<m_{\mathrm{c}},

∥c1(ρ(X1))−c2(ρ(X2)∥≤r|m1−m2|.\|c_{1}(\rho(X_{1}))-c_{2}(\rho(X_{2})\|\leq r|m_{1}-m_{2}|. (25)

Then, under the continuous Lloyd dynamics in (21), the minimal distance of sensors to x∗x^{*} converges to zero, with

m⁡(t)≤eα⁡(r−1)​t​m​(0).m(t)\leq e^{\alpha(r-1)t}m(0).

Proof.

See Appendix 10.

Remark. In Appendix 10, we also show a class of bump functions in which the convergence is global (holding under all initial configurations of sensors). The result above shows that under local Lipschitz continuity condition of the learned importance fields, Lloyd dynamics guarantees the convergence of sensors will converge to x∗x^{*}. Continuity ensures stability of the centroid map and prevents spurious equilibria or oscillations; this highlights the need for importance fields that remain smooth and well-conditioned during closed-loop operation. This underscores the importance of a regular source prediction for the adaptive sensor placement and satisfies our second hypothesis H2.

5.9 Two step optimization procedure

Motivated by the structure adopted in Theorem 1, we adopt a two-scale optimization approach for minimizing the localization functional over the predicted importance fields. We consider the model updates to be a slowly varying external process, such that we can run an inner loop of Lloyd’s updates with guaranteed convergence for a fixed importance, then we update the sensor measurements and model prediction.

Prior approaches to time‑varying coverage control [40, 39, 33, 59] design single-loop control laws that guide agents toward centroids of externally defined, slowly evolving importance fields. In contrast, our method employs a two‑scale update scheme: a fast inner Lloyd’s loop ensures descent of the model‑relative coverage cost for each fixed field, while a slower outer learner updates the importance function based on inference from sparse sensor observations. The density field ρ\rho is evolved via feedback from sensor placements and model predictions.

Explicitly, we define an adaptive sensor placement (outer) loop, wherein the sensor positions X(k)X^{(k)} are fixed and the model predicted importance field ρθ(⋅|zk)\rho_{\theta}(\cdot|z_{k}) is updated according to the sensor data in zkz_{k}. Then we fix the source field and run the discrete Lloyd’s update loop for mm iterations. This two scale optimization process is described in algorithm 2.

6 Numerical experiments

6.1 Data generation

We define a domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} discretized using a conforming triangular finite element mesh, ϕ0\phi^{0}. Synthetic training data are generated by solving steady-state advection-diffusion equations of the form presented in (6) by finite elements over the fine mesh discretization. We consider a compact, local source term parameterized by a bump function with a constant radius for each experiment,

βr​(x)={exp⁡(−r2r2−‖x‖2),‖x‖<r,0,‖x‖≥r.\beta_{r}(x)\;=\;\begin{cases}\displaystyle\exp\!\Bigl(-\dfrac{r^{2}}{\,r^{2}-\|x\|^{2}}\Bigr),&\|x\|<r,\\[5.16663pt] 0,&\|x\|\geq r.\end{cases} (26)

The bump function, βr:ℝd→[0,1]\beta_{r}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to[0,1] is C∞C^{\infty}, equals 11 at the origin, and has compact support strictly inside the ball of radius rr. For each training example, a random set of NN sensors is distributed across Ω\Omega, returning noisy observations of the velocity and scalar field to form the full conditioning input, zz. Together the solution, source, and conditioning inputs form the supervised training dataset, 𝒟:={z(k),u(k),f(k)}k=1ns​a​m​p​l​e​s\mathcal{D}:=\{z^{(k)},u^{(k)},f^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{n_{samples}}. Since all data is from FEM, we are able to quickly generate new samples on the fly to prevent overfitting. We specify an initial cache of ns​a​m​p​l​e​sn_{samples} samples, and update a fixed number of randomly selected samples from this cache after every training iteration, effectively achieving an infinite dataset.

We restrict both source support and sensor placement to an interior subdomain. Let δ>0\delta>0 be a user-defined exclusion distance, and define the valid interior domain

Ωvalid:={𝐱∈Ω|dΩ⁡(𝐱,∂Ω)≥δ}.\Omega_{\mathrm{valid}}:=\left\{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega\;\middle|\;\operatorname{d}_{\Omega}(\mathbf{x},\partial\Omega)\geq\delta\right\}.

This constraint is also applied during the adaptive sampling.

Throughout, we impose a combination of homogeneous Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. To ensure boundary conditions are strongly enforced on the reduced basis, we fix one of the trainable control volumes to represent the known boundary nodes and Dirichlet boundary conditions. Neumann boundary conditions are enforced implicitly.

We evaluate the proposed CNWF model across three benchmark scenarios of increasing geometric complexity: a simple circular domain with variable direction velocity, a regular mesh over the Gulf of Mexico with flow data coming from reanalysis simulations, and a maze geometry with simulated stokes flow following the path of the maze. These scenarios also correspond to different underlying hydrodynamic models, ℳ\mathcal{M} in (1), ranging from a nominal flow to a full physical model. In each case we used a fixed number of randomly distributed sensors, placed independently for each training and test sample. Additionally, in each case we have a source of variability; the velocity direction for the circular geometry and the Péclet number for the Gulf and maze geometries. We note all cases have not been designed to match a particular physical scenario, but rather to convey the benefits of the CNWF localization method on challenging benchmarks.

6.2 Baselines

To assess the benefit of structure preservation, we compare CNWF against two conventional black-box baselines: a standard multilayer perceptron (MLP) and an identical transformer model to the CNWF encoder with a linear layer to output, both trained to predict the source field directly from the sensor data with positive outputs from ReLU activations and normalized to a distribution following (17). The MLP provides a minimal complexity neural network parameterization, but as we will demonstrate struggles to capture the complex inverse process. The transformer baseline is identical to the encoder core of the CNWF model but lacks the head networks and structure preservation.

7 Results

To verify the performance of the CNWF approach we first consider the inverse source identification problem alone then demonstrate its effectiveness when coupled with the adaptive sensor placement algorithm. We demonstrate accurate source reconstruction from limited, noisy measurements, and empirical convergence to the true source location under the adaptive sensor placement strategy. In all cases we evaluate the models on samples draw randomly from the same parameter distribution used to generate the training data.

7.1 Inverse problem

We demonstrate the ability of the CNWF model to produce accurate and interpretable source distribution predictions from the sparse sensor measurements by considering architected and intentionally ill-posed scenarios shown in Figures 2, and 3. In these scenarios we consider collinear sensor locations transversing the circular domain; when all sensors are located off the informative region within the advective plume, the SNR is lower and accurate prediction is infeasible. In both cases, the CNWF model produces smooth, interpretable, and qualitatively accurate source distributions, even in the ill-posed configurations. This also results in the lowest error as measured by the W2W_{2} metric, in some cases by an order of magnitude over the baseline transformer. This confirms our first hypothesis H1, that the physical structure provides a useful inductive bias for training.

In Figure 4 we compare the average predicted source density for each model, over 1024 random sensor configurations. We note that while the CNWF and transformer baseline both capture the area of highest probability, corresponding to the true source location, the CNWF localizes the source better on average, and provides a smoother source field.

We hypothesis that the regularity of the CNWF generated predictions is the use of the adaptive basis functions, which implicitly bias the model towards better localization. We visualize the basis functions for a sample source and sensor configuration on the circular domain in Figure 5. A shared basis is used to represent the source and solution during training. We note the correspondence of a single partition to the source location (ψ40\psi_{4}^{0}) while others correspond to the predicted downstream solution.

To assess physical consistency we evaluate the full inverse-forward process. The inverse model returns a normalized source density f^θ​(𝐱)=ρθ​(𝐱|z)\hat{f}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\rho_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\,|\,z); we input this prediction into the original steady advection–diffusion equation (6) using the true velocity field 𝐯\mathbf{v} and Péclet number. This is then solved using the same FEM discretization on the fine mesh as for the data generation, producing the reconstructed scalar field u~\tilde{u}. Consistency is quantified by the normalized MSE between the reconstructed solution and true solution using a normalized input source,

Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​y=‖u~−utrue‖L2​(Ω)‖utrue‖L2​(Ω).E_{consistency}\;=\;\frac{\bigl\|\,\tilde{u}-u_{\mathrm{true}}\bigr\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}}{\bigl\|u_{\mathrm{true}}\bigr\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}}.

Note that for the CNWF model, this is distinct from the forward FEM solve using the learned nonlinear flux. We compare Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​yE_{consistency} for the the CNWF and baseline models in Figure 6 and give sample solutions in the circular domain in Figure 7. We observe that in addition to yielding more accurate source predictions, the CNWF model provides a source term which is more compatible with the original PDE. This is most pronounced in the circular domain experiment.

We vary the number of sensors NN to evaluate how prediction accuracy scales with sensor count. Despite being trained on a fixed number of sensors, the model exhibits strong generalization to varying sensor counts due to the permutation-invariant architecture of the transformer encoder. As shown in Fig 8, the average prediction error for the inferred source fhf_{h} decreases monotonically with the number of available sensors. This reflects the model’s ability to effectively integrate information across an expanding set of observations, even without retraining. While the error does not converge to zero due to factors such as measurement noise, limited spatial coverage, and model representational capacity, the trend confirms that the architecture maintains stable performance under partial supervision and supports variable sensor deployment in practical applications. We note the CNWF improves faster with additional sensors than the transformer baseline, and reaches a lower minimum.

In Theorem 3 we hypothesize that reducing the true coverage error results in more informative sensor configurations, and therefore improved error bounds on the source prediction task. We additionally analyze model performance as a function of the average observed field magnitude at sensor locations:

u¯obs=1N​∑i=1N|u⁡(𝐱i)|.\bar{u}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|u(\mathbf{x}_{i})|.

We interpret u¯obs\bar{u}_{\text{obs}} as an empirical proxy for the local observability of the source, with higher values indicating stronger coupling between sensors and the underlying field dynamics. In the presence of noise, this directly correlates to the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where higher sensor value indicates a lower SNR.

As shown in Fig. 9, decreased 𝒥t​r​u​e\mathcal{J}_{true} and increased uo​b​su_{obs} both result in reduced source prediction error, suggesting that access to higher quality measurements improves inference. The observed dependence of accuracy on 𝒥t​r​u​e\mathcal{J}_{true} motivates the use of the adaptive coverage objective described in section 5.9, under the condition in 3.

7.2 Nonlinear Advection Diffusion

To demonstrate the generality of the CNWF to a general class of transport processes we also consider a nonlinear advection diffusion system, with

𝐯⁡(u):={0u⁡(x)<T,𝐯0​α​u​(x)u⁡(x)>T.\mathbf{v}(u):=\begin{cases}0&u(x)<T,\\ \mathbf{v}_{0}\alpha u(x)&u(x)>T.\end{cases} (27)

and demonstrate similar, improved performance in this setting, as shown in table 1.

7.3 Adaptive sensor placement

We evaluate the ability of the proposed method to improve source localization by iteratively refining sensor positions using the geodesic Lloyd algorithm. Starting from a fixed initial configuration, sensors are repositioned over KK outer iterations, using the model-predicted source density ρθ(⋅∣zk)\rho_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z_{k}) as an importance function. We track both the model-relative objective Jρk​(X)J_{\rho_{k}}(X) and the true localization error Jtrue​(X)J_{\mathrm{true}}(X) across iterations. Sample trajectories for a single randomly selected case on each geometry is shown in Figure 10

In Figure 11 we compare the average prediction errors (by Wasserstein metric) for random initializations and after running the two step adaptive sampling algorithm described in Algorithm 2. In all cases adaptive sampling improves the final source identification. The CNWF model outperforms the baselines both before and after sensor positioning, and demonstrates the largest proportional improvement from adaptive sampling. We note that the changes due to sensor positioning are smaller than the differences between model class, indicating that while good sensor placement is clearly necessary, model capability is a larger limiting factor. This underscores the need for a principled training procedure such as in the CNWF implementation.

Figure 12 reports normalized values of both 𝒥ρk\mathcal{J}_{\rho_{k}} and 𝒥true\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{true}} as a function of iteration kk for the circular domain over 20 trials. Model updates to ρk\rho_{k} are applied on iterations 5, 11, and 17. We observe near-monotonic improvement in all test cases, suggesting that the CNWF-predicted source field remains stable and informative throughout the adaptive loop. The change in coverage objective is shown in Figure 13.

This closed-loop behavior confirms the benefit of integrating structure-preserving inference with sensor guidance: learned source predictions not only match the observed field but also serve as actionable importance maps for adaptive coverage. As shown in Table 2, this process improves final source prediction accuracy across all geometries. The improvement is most pronounced in the circular domain, where velocity variability is high and field observations alone are less informative without adaptive refinement. The key metrics are summarized in table 2.

8 Discussion and conclusions

We presented a structure-preserving framework for source identification in advection–diffusion systems, coupling finite element exterior calculus with neural network surrogates to recover spatially distributed source terms from sparse sensor measurements. The proposed CNWF model integrates learned source and flux terms within a PDE-constrained optimization framework that maintains compatibility with the underlying conservation law. The data-adaptive reduced basis, provides efficient inference while retaining physical consistency.

Our analysis established conditions under which the adaptive sensor placement loop, based on geodesic Lloyd’s algorithm, converges in both model-relative and true coverage objectives. In particular, we proved that if the change in the predicted importance function is bounded relative to the descent achieved in the Lloyd update, then the overall sensing configuration strictly improves. This feedback loop was shown to reduce prediction error bounds under mild regularity assumptions, providing theoretical support for the closed-loop design.

Empirical results across three domains demonstrate that CNWF achieves improved source prediction and consistency with the true PDE compared to baseline MLP and transformer models. Notably, the CNWF model exhibits strong generalization to unseen sensor configurations, improved localization through adaptive sampling, and smooth, interpretable source fields. These benefits result from structure preservation, reduced basis representation, and physically motivated training constraints. Together, these results validate CNWF as a principled and effective tool for inverse modeling and adaptive sensing in transport systems.

Appendix A: Neural Network Parameterization Details

We parameterize the source, flux, and basis terms in eq. 15 using neural networks conditioned on sparse sensor measurements. The CNWF approach provides a structure-preserving framework that admits flexible neural parameterizations. The key properties that must be preserved are the POU property of the basis functions, and the non-negativity of the learned source. The anti-symmetry of the fluxes is automatically achieved through the coboundary operator.

We implement the parameterizations as task specific head networks around a universal transformer encoder, which contains ∼\sim90% of the parameters of the composite CNWF model. This maps from the conditioning inputs to a latent representation and allows for a shared representation of the underlying physical problem setting across the partition, flux, and source networks.. Let z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} denote the vector of sensor inputs, which is encoded by the permutation-invariant transformer encoder ℰθ:ℝdz→ℝdz^,\mathcal{E}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\hat{z}}}, yielding a latent representation z^=ℰθ​(z)∈ℝdz^\hat{z}=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\hat{z}}}.

The reduced-basis source term is predicted by a network 𝒮θ:ℝdz^→ℝnc0,\mathcal{S}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\hat{z}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}^{0}}, so that the learned source coefficients are given by f^θ​(z):=𝒮θ​(z^)≥0\hat{f}_{\theta}(z):=\mathcal{S}_{\theta}(\hat{z})\geq 0. We enforce non-negative outputs through a ReLU activation on the final layer. The flux correction in the reduced 1-form space is predicted by a network 𝒩θ:ℝnc0×ℝdz^→ℝnc1,\mathcal{N}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}^{0}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{\hat{z}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}^{1}}, with output defined as 𝒩θ​(u^,z):=𝒩θ​(u^,z^)\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\hat{u},z):=\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\hat{u},\hat{z}), where u^\hat{u} are the reduced scalar field coefficients. Finally, the basis transformation is defined by a network 𝒫θ:ℝdz^→ℝnc0×nf0,\mathcal{P}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\hat{z}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}^{0}\times n_{f}^{0}}, producing a convex combination matrix via row-wise softmax: Wθ​(z):=softmaxrow​(𝒫θ​(z^)).W_{\theta}(z):=\text{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\mathcal{P}_{\theta}(\hat{z})\right).

In this work, we use a self-attention transformer to encode the sensor data, an MLP for the source term, a modified residual network for the fluxes, and cross attention with the spatial node coordinates for the partition network, for more detail see Appendix Appendix C: Model and Training Parameters. The flux networks are implemented in a residual architecture comprising a linear skip connection and a nonlinear MLP,

𝒩θ​(u^,z)=ℒ⁡(u^,z)+α​𝒩n​o​n​l​i​n​e​a​r​(u^,z),\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\hat{u},z)=\mathcal{L}(\hat{u},z)+\alpha\mathcal{N}_{nonlinear}(\hat{u},z),

with a tunable gain parameter α>0\alpha>0 that controls the contribution of the nonlinear component and balances expressivity with numerical stability. A schematic representation of the neural network parameterization is shown in Figure 1.

We note that this approach is amendable to supervised pretraining via the transformer backbone, which can then be fine tuned through the head networks into a structure preserving model. This approach greatly reduces the number of training iterations that require a full nonlinear solve but may introduce undesirable local minima when transitioning to the structure preserving phase. We did not pretrain in this work.

All networks are implemented in pyTorch [52] and optimized using Adam [37]. All terms are differentiable and trainable via auto-differentiation. The CNWF model for each test case was trained on a Nvidia H200, for ∼\sim3 hours wall time per example.

Transformer Encoder

A full description of the partition transformer architecture is provided in [36], and closely follows a standard cross-attention encoder. For completeness we describe our sensor encoding transformer backbone implementation here, which is built on a standard multihead self attention architecture. Let z={zi}i=1Nz=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} be a set of sensor observations, where each zi=(xi,ui,𝐯i)∈ℝdz_{i}=(x_{i},u_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} encodes spatial location, scalar field value, and local velocity. We project each ziz_{i} into a token hi(0)∈ℝdtokenh_{i}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{token}}} via a learned linear embedding layer.

The encoder ℰϕ\mathcal{E}_{\phi} is composed of LL stacked transformer blocks. Each block applies multi-head self-attention followed by an MLP with residual connections:

H(ℓ+1)\displaystyle H^{(\ell+1)} =LayerNorm​(H(ℓ)+MultiHeadSelfAttention​(H(ℓ))),\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}\left(H^{(\ell)}+\text{MultiHeadSelfAttention}(H^{(\ell)})\right),
H(ℓ+1)\displaystyle H^{(\ell+1)} =LayerNorm​(H(ℓ+1)+MLP​(H(ℓ+1))),\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}\left(H^{(\ell+1)}+\text{MLP}(H^{(\ell+1)})\right),

where H(ℓ)={hi(ℓ)}i=1NH^{(\ell)}=\{h_{i}^{(\ell)}\}_{i=1}^{N}, and attention is computed using:

Attention​(Q,K,V)=softmax​(Q​K⊤dhead)​V.\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}}\right)V.

After the final attention layer, we obtain updated tokens {hi(L)}\{h_{i}^{(L)}\}. These are pooled into a global latent z^∈ℝdz\hat{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} using attention pooling:

z^=∑i=1Nαi​hi(L),αi=exp⁡(w⊤​hi(L))∑jexp⁡(w⊤​hj(L)),\hat{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{i}h_{i}^{(L)},\quad\alpha_{i}=\frac{\exp(w^{\top}h_{i}^{(L)})}{\sum_{j}\exp(w^{\top}h_{j}^{(L)})},

with w∈ℝdtokenw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{token}}} learned during training.

This encoder is permutation-invariant by design and supports variable-size input sets.

Appendix B: Data setup

All data were generated by solving the FEM discretization of the advection diffusion equations using the scikit-fem [23] python package. Meshes were generated using gmsh [21], or nanomesh [56]. Each mesh has O⁡(1​e​3)~O(1e3) nodes, although we note the reduced basis allows efficient generalization to finer discretizations. Velocitiy profiles for the Gulf were retrieved from NOAA [27], and for the maze were generated by solving stokes flow in scikit-fem with inlet and outlet boundary conditions. We use homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries throughout, with Neumann conditions imposed on the outlet of the maze and gulf. We parameterize the source term with a bump function with radius r=0.07r=0.07. We chose Péclet 1​e​3~1e3 for all examples to give qualitatively interesting results while maintaining stability for the chosen discretization and solver. The discretized domains, and sample velocities, forcings, and resulting scalar fields are shown for each experiment in Figure 14.

Appendix C: Model and Training Parameters

All models use the same general architecture and training setup unless otherwise noted. Each model was implemented in PyTorch and trained in double precision. ReLU activations were used throughout both the transformer encoder and MLP head networks. A constant dropout rate of 0 was used across all layers. All optimization was performed using Adam with default PyTorch settings.

The table below summarizes the model architecture and training hyperparameters used across experiments.

We now provide a general class of functions which satisfy (28) for all configurations XX, ensuring global convergence of sensors to x∗x^{*}. This class of functions places a nonzero mass across the entire domain, to ensure the centroid formula (5.5) for cells not containing the event is well-defined and approximately solves the unweighted coverage problem.

The main task in constructing such functions is ensuring that there is a universal lower bound on the fraction of mass from ρX\rho_{X} contained in V∗V^{*}. We will use bump functions. By this, we say that φ\varphi is a bump function if it is a nonnegative smooth function with support contained in the unit disk centered at the origin and ∫ℝ2φ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\varphi(x)dx=1. It is also required to satisfy a sector condition: there exists α>0\alpha>0 such that for any sector KθK_{\theta} of the unit circle at the origin with angle θ\theta,

∫Kθφ​𝑑x≥α​θ.\int_{K_{\theta}}\varphi dx\geq\alpha\theta. (37)

The sector condition holds for a large collection of functions. For instance, φ\varphi can be radially symmetric, or have a support which contains a disk of any size centered about the origin.

We consider bump functions containing x∗x^{*} having support D:=Dr′​m​(x∗)D:=D_{r^{\prime}m}(x^{*}) (a disk of radius r′​mr^{\prime}m centered at x∗x^{*}). Outside of the support, the function is a sufficiently small constant β\beta which makes the dynamics and defined, and reduces to unweighted Lloyd dynamics in cells outside of the bump function’s support. For a bump function φ\varphi and r′∈(0,1)r^{\prime}\in(0,1), the importance function takes the form of a translated and scaled copy of φ\varphi with background noise:

ρP​(x)={1(r′​m)2​φ​(qr′​m)q∈D,βq∈Ω\D.\rho_{P}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{(r^{\prime}m)^{2}}\varphi\left(\frac{q}{r^{\prime}m}\right)&q\in D,\\ \beta&q\in\Omega\backslash D.\end{cases} (38)
